title: What Is the Silk Mark, and How Do You Check One?
description: What the Silk Mark hologram certifies, who issues it, how to verify a tag, and what it means when an older saree does not have one.

seo.title: What Is the Silk Mark? How to Check One | From The Trunk
seo.description: What the Silk Mark hologram certifies, who issues it, how to verify a tag, and what it means when an older saree does not have one.

cover.alt: Hands holding a small holographic tag on the border of a maroon and gold zari saree

body.text: The Silk Mark is India's certification for pure natural silk. It takes the form of a small hologram label with a unique number, and it is issued by the Silk Mark Organisation of India, a body set up under the Central Silk Board. A genuine tag means the fabric it is attached to has been certified as pure silk, not a blend or a synthetic.
It is the closest thing to a plain answer in a market where a great many things are described as silk.
What does the Silk Mark certify?
The label certifies fibre content. It confirms the fabric is pure natural silk.

It is worth being clear about what it does not tell you. It says nothing about the quality of the weaving, whether the zari is real metal, where the saree was made, or what it is worth. A Silk Mark tag on a plain silk saree and one on a handwoven Kanjeevaram certify exactly the same fact.
How do you check a Silk Mark tag?
Look for three things.
**The hologram.** A genuine label has a holographic element that shifts as you tilt it. A flat printed copy does not.
**The unique number.** Every genuine label carries one. It is not decorative.
**The seller.** Silk Mark labels are issued to authorised users, so the tag should be attached by the shop or weaver who sold it, not loose in the bag.
The Silk Mark Organisation runs chapters across India and provides testing services, which is the route to take if you have a piece you are seriously unsure about.

body.text: Why do so many pure silk sarees have no Silk Mark?
This is the part that confuses people, and it matters enormously if you are buying preloved.

The Silk Mark scheme became widely used in the 2000s. Sarees woven before that, which includes a great many of the finest pieces still in circulation, were never tagged. Tags also get cut off, fall away, or are removed when a saree is dry cleaned.

So a missing Silk Mark is not evidence of anything. On a vintage saree it is the norm. What it means is that the other checks matter more, and that the honesty of whoever is selling it matters most of all.
What should you do when there is no tag?

Run the ordinary tests. Tilt it under a light and watch whether the sheen shifts colour. Rub a section between your palms and feel for warmth. Look at the reverse for the small irregularities of a handloom. Then scrape a loose end of zari gently. Pure zari stays silver right through, while copper underneath means tested zari. Our guide on [how to identify a pure silk saree](/journal/how-to-identify-pure-silk-saree) covers every test in detail.
If it is a significant purchase and none of that settles it, accredited testing is available and worth the trouble.
Is a Silk Mark essential when buying preloved?

The Silk Mark is useful and worth looking for on anything new. On preloved and vintage sarees it is a welcome bonus, not a requirement, and its absence should not put you off a piece that passes every other check.
